notes.b: Textiles are used throughout the home for practical and decorative purposes, often several at once.
points: Warmth and insulation: blankets, duvets and throws trap still air within their fibres and layers, reducing heat loss from the body.
Sound absorption: carpets, rugs, curtains and upholstery absorb sound and reduce echo in a room.
Privacy and light control: curtains and blinds screen the room from view and control the light entering it.
Comfort: cushions, mattress covers and upholstery give softness and support.
Protection: oven gloves and aprons protect the user from heat and spills, and carpets protect floors from wear.
Absorbency: towels and bath mats take up water from the body or from the floor.
Decoration: curtains, cushions, wall hangings and bedspreads add colour, pattern and texture to a room.
Hygiene: washable textiles can be laundered to remove dirt and micro-organisms.

notes.b: A textile is chosen by weighing the properties of the fabric against the job it has to do, the money available and the household's preferences.
points: Fitness for purpose: the fabric's properties must suit its job, e.g. a towel needs absorbency and a curtain needs to drape well and resist fading.
Suitability in use: the fabric must withstand the wear, washing and conditions of the room it is used in, such as a kitchen or a child's bedroom.
Cost: the price of the fabric must fit the budget; natural fibres such as wool and silk cost more than most synthetic fibres.
Personal choice: colour, style, comfort and a preference for natural or easy-care fabrics.
Aesthetic appeal: appearance, texture, drape, lustre, colour and pattern.
Ease of care: the washing, drying and ironing a fabric needs affects how practical it is for the household.

notes.h: Fabric properties that matter in the home
points: Absorbent: the fabric takes in and holds moisture; cotton and linen are absorbent, which makes them suitable for towels.
Flammable: the fabric ignites and burns readily when exposed to a flame, creating a fire risk.
Crease-resistant: the fabric resists wrinkling in use and in washing and returns towards its smooth shape, so less ironing is needed.
Colourfast: the colour resists running in water and fading in light, so it stays bright after washing; the dye must be fixed firmly to the fibres.
Durable: the fabric resists abrasion, tearing and wear over a long period of use.
Drape: the way a fabric hangs in folds; a good drape suits curtains and loose clothing.
Cotton towels: absorbent, strong when wet and able to withstand hot washing.
Linen tea towels: absorbent, strong and quick drying, but creases easily unless treated.
Polyester curtains: drape well, resist fading, wash easily and resist creasing.
Cotton curtains: easy to launder and dye, with a crisp appearance, but shrink if not pre-shrunk.
Wool blankets: warm, insulating, absorbent and elastic, but can shrink and felt if washed at high temperatures.
Nylon carpets: strong, hard wearing and resistant to abrasion from foot traffic.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that a textile's properties must match the job it is required to do in the home.
The ability of a fabric to take in and hold moisture.
The tendency of a fabric to ignite and burn readily when exposed to a flame.
The ability of a fabric to resist wrinkling and recover its smooth shape during use and washing.
The ability of a fabric's colour to resist running in water and fading in light.
The way a fabric hangs and falls in folds under its own weight.
The ability of a fabric to withstand wear, abrasion and tearing over a long period of use.
The visual and tactile qualities of a textile, such as colour, pattern, texture and lustre, that make it attractive.

factCards.definition: Polyester: it drapes well, is fade resistant, washes easily and resists creasing.

factCards.term: Property of untreated fabric that creates a fire risk
factCards.definition: Flammability: an untreated fabric ignites and burns readily when exposed to a flame.

factCards.definition: Cotton and linen: both are absorbent and washable.

questions.prompt: Identify three functions of textiles used in a living room and give one example of a textile for each function.
questions.model: Any three of: warmth or insulation (a wool throw or rug); sound absorption (a carpet or heavy curtains); privacy (lined curtains or blinds); comfort (cushions or upholstered sofa); decoration (wall hangings or a patterned curtain); protection (a rug protecting the floor from wear).

questions.prompt: Explain how cost, fitness for purpose and personal choice influence a household's choice of textiles. Give an example for each factor.
questions.model: Fitness for purpose: a textile's properties must match its use, e.g. a towel must be absorbent and strong when wet, so cotton is chosen; a curtain must drape well and resist fading, so polyester is chosen. Cost: natural fibres such as wool and silk are more expensive than most synthetic fibres, so a family with a limited budget may choose a cheaper polyester or cotton blend for everyday items. Personal choice: preferences for colour, style, comfort and easy-care fabrics affect the choice, e.g. a household that wants low maintenance chooses a crease-resistant synthetic blend for bed linen. The factors often pull against each other, e.g. a cheap fabric may not have the properties the purpose requires, so the household must weigh cost against fitness for purpose.
